ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: The study received ethical approval from the Coordinating Ethics Committee of Helsinki and Uusimaa Hospital District (94/13/03/00/09, HUS/1204/2017) and Swedish Ethical Review Authority (2020-07058), with all participants providing written informed consent.

Participants were recruited from prior national surveys, with inclusion criteria set at ages 60-77, a CAIDE Dementia Risk Score 18 of at least six points, and cognitive function at or just below mean levels for their age.
table.formatted: Participants were recruited from prior national surveys, with inclusion criteria set at ages 60-77, a CAIDE Dementia Risk Score <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> of at least six points, and cognitive function at or just below mean levels for their age.

table.text: Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either the intervention group (intensive multidomain lifestyle program) or the control group (standard health advice).

Post-randomization, control participants were given routine health advice and risk factor information during main study visits at six months, one year, and two years, along with instructions to consult healthcare providers as needed.
Six additional meetings provided further measurements and lifestyle guidance, with no medications prescribed; participants were advised to reach out to healthcare providers if necessary.
Of the 1260 individuals randomized, 1,190 participants were included in the modified intention-to-treat (mITT) population, as previously defined by Ngandu et al 9 .

table.text: For longitudinal cognitive analyses, participants were required to have baseline cognition and at least one cognitive assessment at either the 1-or 2-year follow-up.

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> Participants were recruited from prior national surveys, with inclusion criteria set at ages 60-77, a CAIDE Dementia Risk Score 18 of at least six points, and cognitive function at or just below mean levels for their age.

> Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either the intervention group (intensive multidomain lifestyle program) or the control group (standard health advice).

> Post-randomization, control participants were given routine health advice and risk factor information during main study visits at six months, one year, and two years, along with instructions to consult healthcare providers as needed.

> Six additional meetings provided further measurements and lifestyle guidance, with no medications prescribed; participants were advised to reach out to healthcare providers if necessary.

> Of the 1260 individuals randomized, 1,190 participants were included in the modified intention-to-treat (mITT) population, as previously defined by Ngandu et al 9 .

> For longitudinal cognitive analyses, participants were required to have baseline cognition and at least one cognitive assessment at either the 1-or 2-year follow-up.

Ethics approval statement:

> The study received ethical approval from the Coordinating Ethics Committee of Helsinki and Uusimaa Hospital District (94/13/03/00/09, HUS/1204/2017) and Swedish Ethical Review Authority (2020-07058), with all participants providing written informed consent.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: The FINGER trial demonstrated that a multidomain lifestyle intervention benefits cognition in older adults at-risk of dementia, yet the underlying biological mechanisms remain unclear.

We measured neurodegeneration-related proteins using the NULISAseq CNS disease panel in 1158 FINGER participants to investigate associations between circulating proteins, cognitive trajectories, and intervention response.
Independent of the intervention, ten proteins spanning immune, neuronal, and metabolic processes were associated with poorer cognitive trajectories, with TREM2 among the strongest signals.
The intervention led to changes in eight proteins, including CRH, IL-7 and MME.
Eleven proteins modified the cognitive response to intervention, with KDR and CRH showing the strongest effect.
Complementary Elastic Net analyses confirmed CRH, and further identified PTN and CCL2 as markers of intervention responsiveness.
Additional proteins showed APOE ε4-and sex-specific associations with the intervention response.
Together, these findings identify proteomic signatures of cognitive response that could inform precision dementia prevention.

The growing global burden of Alzheimer's disease and related disorders (ADRD) represents a profound health challenge, underscoring the need for effective interventions for preserving cognitive function among people at risk of dementia.
ADRDs are driven by complex disease mechanisms 1 , with modifiable lifestyle and health-related factors accounting for an estimated 45% of the overall risk 2 .
text.formatted: ADRDs are driven by complex disease mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">1</ref> , with modifiable lifestyle and health-related factors accounting for an estimated 45% of the overall risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> .

text.text: Despite recent advances in disease-modifying therapies for early Alzheimer's disease (AD), available treatments have modest clinical effects, are restricted to selected patient groups, and remain challenging to implement at population level [3] [4] [5] .
text.formatted: Despite recent advances in disease-modifying therapies for early Alzheimer's disease (AD), available treatments have modest clinical effects, are restricted to selected patient groups, and remain challenging to implement at population level <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> .

text.text: Thus, lifestyle-based interventions have emerged as a promising strategy to mitigate cognitive decline and potentially delay the onset of ADRD, as emphasized in the updated 2026 WHO guidelines on dementia risk reduction 6 .
text.formatted: Thus, lifestyle-based interventions have emerged as a promising strategy to mitigate cognitive decline and potentially delay the onset of ADRD, as emphasized in the updated 2026 WHO guidelines on dementia risk reduction <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6</ref> .

text.text: Dietary patterns, physical activity, cognitive and social engagement, and effective management of vascular and metabolic risk factors have all been linked to better cognitive health and reduced dementia risk 2, 6, 7 .
text.formatted: Dietary patterns, physical activity, cognitive and social engagement, and effective management of vascular and metabolic risk factors have all been linked to better cognitive health and reduced dementia risk <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7</ref> .

text.text: The Finnish Geriatric Intervention Study to Prevent Cognitive Impairment and Disability (FINGER) was the first clinical trial which provided proof of concept that targeting these factors simultaneously can improve cognition and exert other related health benefits in older adults at increased risk of dementia 8, 9 .
text.formatted: The Finnish Geriatric Intervention Study to Prevent Cognitive Impairment and Disability (FINGER) was the first clinical trial which provided proof of concept that targeting these factors simultaneously can improve cognition and exert other related health benefits in older adults at increased risk of dementia <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> .

text.text: This two-year landmark trial initiated the World-Wide FINGERS (WW-FINGERS) network of multidomain dementia risk reduction trials 10 throughout which the initial FINGER findings have been replicated in other geographical and cultural settings (e.g., in North America, US-POINTER 11 and South America, Latam-FINGERS 12 ).
text.formatted: This two-year landmark trial initiated the World-Wide FINGERS (WW-FINGERS) network of multidomain dementia risk reduction trials <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">10</ref> throughout which the initial FINGER findings have been replicated in other geographical and cultural settings (e.g., in North America, US-POINTER <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11</ref> and South America, Latam-FINGERS <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12</ref> ).

text.text: Yet an important question remains: what happens biologically when such an intervention has an impact on cognitive function, and why do some individuals benefit more than others?
Blood-based biomarkers provide a window into these processes.

The rapid advances in the biomarker field offer important insights into cognitive health and present significant opportunities for understanding and further developing the early intervention strategies in the context of ADRD.
Plasma phosphorylated tau, amyloid-β, glial fibrillary acidic protein and neurofilament light are biomarkers currently used for tracking neuropathological and neurodegenerative processes 13, 14 .
text.formatted: Plasma phosphorylated tau, amyloid-β, glial fibrillary acidic protein and neurofilament light are biomarkers currently used for tracking neuropathological and neurodegenerative processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">14</ref> .

text.text: However, these established markers capture only a fraction of the molecular changes associated with cognitive aging and early neurodegenerative processes and may provide limited information on the broader biological mechanisms through which multidomain lifestyle interventions exert their effects 15 .
text.formatted: However, these established markers capture only a fraction of the molecular changes associated with cognitive aging and early neurodegenerative processes and may provide limited information on the broader biological mechanisms through which multidomain lifestyle interventions exert their effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">15</ref> .

text.text: Therefore, circulating proteins reflecting other molecular pathways that are central to brain health, such as inflammation, vascular function, metabolic homeostasis, and synaptic integrity, may help to understand how lifestyle interventions affect systemic and brain-related biology.
They may also help identify individuals most likely to benefit from these interventions.
In this study, we characterized circulating protein profiles using the highly-sensitive, state-of-the-art NULISA technology 16 (NULISAseq™ CNS Disease 120 panel) in the FINGER trial.
text.formatted: In this study, we characterized circulating protein profiles using the highly-sensitive, state-of-the-art NULISA technology <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">16</ref> (NULISAseq™ CNS Disease 120 panel) in the FINGER trial.

text.text: The panel included both established ADRD biomarkers and a broader set of mostly less explored multi-mechanistic proteins.
In a separate work we focused on the core markers 17 ; here, we focused on proteins reflecting broader disease biology.
text.formatted: In a separate work we focused on the core markers <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">17</ref> ; here, we focused on proteins reflecting broader disease biology.

text.text: We first investigated the associations of these proteins with cognitive performance and cognitive change in the whole population.

We further evaluated intervention-related changes in protein levels over time, identified baseline proteins associated with intervention responsiveness and examined whether these associations differed according to APOE ε4 carrier status and sex.
Established ADRD biomarkers were examined separately as reference markers in correlation analyses.
To capture the multidimensional nature of biological responses, we applied machine learning approaches to identify protein signatures predictive of intervention response.

Finally, baseline protein profiles were compared between intervention-adherent responders and non-responders to identify molecular pathways associated with successful cognitive benefit from the lifestyle intervention.

This research constitutes an exploratory analysis of the FINGER RCT (ClinicalTrials.gov ID NCT01041989), which evaluated the effectiveness of a multidomain lifestyle intervention on cognition among community-dwelling older adults at risk for dementia across six centers in Finland (N=1260, average age 69 years at baseline).
Screening and baseline evaluations occurred between September 2009 and November 2011, and the core two-year RCT was completed in February 2014.
Details on the FINGER protocol, and main trial findings are available elsewhere 8, 9 .
text.formatted: Details on the FINGER protocol, and main trial findings are available elsewhere <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> .

text.text: The study received ethical approval from the Coordinating Ethics Committee of Helsinki and Uusimaa Hospital District (94/13/03/00/09, HUS/1204/2017) and Swedish Ethical Review Authority (2020-07058), with all participants providing written informed consent.

Participants were recruited from prior national surveys, with inclusion criteria set at ages 60-77, a CAIDE Dementia Risk Score 18 of at least six points, and cognitive function at or just below mean levels for their age.
text.formatted: Participants were recruited from prior national surveys, with inclusion criteria set at ages 60-77, a CAIDE Dementia Risk Score <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">18</ref> of at least six points, and cognitive function at or just below mean levels for their age.

text.text: Key exclusion criteria included previously diagnosed or suspected dementia, significant cognitive impairment (Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) <20), and conditions that could compromise safe participation.
text.formatted: Key exclusion criteria included previously diagnosed or suspected dementia, significant cognitive impairment (Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) <20), and conditions that could compromise safe participation.

text.text: This selection process aimed to represent the general Finnish older population with dementia risk factors but minimal cognitive impairment 19.
text.formatted: This selection process aimed to represent the general Finnish older population with dementia risk factors but minimal cognitive impairment <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19</ref>.

text.text: Participants were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either the intervention group (intensive multidomain lifestyle program) or the control group (standard health advice).
Randomization was executed using computer-generated allocations in blocks of four at each site (two participants to each group).
Efforts were made to achieve double-blinding, with outcome assessors unaware of intervention specifics and group allocations remaining undisclosed.
The primary outcome was change in global cognition measured by a total composite z-score from the Neuropsychological Test Battery (NTB).
After two years, the intervention group exhibited greater cognitive improvement compared to controls and a reduced risk of cognitive decline. 9
text.formatted: After two years, the intervention group exhibited greater cognitive improvement compared to controls and a reduced risk of cognitive decline. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref>

text.text: All participants received baseline lifestyle information (mini-intervention) and feedback regarding their vascular risk factors.

Post-randomization, control participants were given routine health advice and risk factor information during main study visits at six months, one year, and two years, along with instructions to consult healthcare providers as needed.
Those in the intervention group engaged in a comprehensive program encompassing dietary counseling, physical activity, cognitive stimulation, and monitoring of vascular and metabolic factors.
The intervention details are described elsewhere 8, 9 .
text.formatted: The intervention details are described elsewhere <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref> .

text.text: Interventions were delivered by a multidisciplinary team in accordance with national and international guidelines.

Intervention adherence was assessed according to a prespecified definition 20 based on participation in the activities offered to the intervention group, with high adherence defined as >50% overall participation across intervention domains.
text.formatted: Intervention adherence was assessed according to a prespecified definition <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">20</ref> based on participation in the activities offered to the intervention group, with high adherence defined as >50% overall participation across intervention domains.

text.text: In summary, the dietary intervention included three individual sessions and six to eight group sessions tailored to participants' needs.
The exercise component included progressive strength training (one to three weekly group sessions) alongside individualized aerobic training (two to five weekly sessions).

Cognitive training encompassed ten group sessions (educational content) and individualized computerbased activities (in two six-month blocks, training three times weekly), targeting executive function, memory, and processing speed with distinct tasks from outcome assessments.
Management of metabolic and vascular risks sought to enhance blood pressure, lipids, glucose, and weight, adhering to national care guidelines.
Six additional meetings provided further measurements and lifestyle guidance, with no medications prescribed; participants were advised to reach out to healthcare providers if necessary.
Cognitive assessments using the NTB were carried out by blinded psychologists at baseline, one year, and two years.
The trial's primary outcome was the change in the NTB total score, representing global cognition (mean of 14 tests, with at least eight required for calculations).
Scores at each timepoint were converted to z-scores standardized to baseline mean and SD (higher scores indicating better performance).
Detailed description of the cognitive assessment has been published elsewhere 9.
text.formatted: Detailed description of the cognitive assessment has been published elsewhere <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9</ref>.

text.text: Fasting venous blood samples were obtained at baseline, six months, one year, and two years.

Serum and plasma were separated immediately, frozen, and transferred monthly to the Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare laboratory, where samples were aliquoted and stored at -70°C for future analysis.
APOE genotype was assessed using standard techniques 21 .

text.text: An Elastic net regression pipeline was implemented to test whether biomarkers identified through mixed-effects models remained predictive within a multivariable machine learning framework that accounts for correlations between predictors.

This approach identifies sets of biomarkers that jointly predict cognitive change over two years, and, separately, biomarkers whose association with cognitive change depends on the intervention group.
Elastic net combines L1 (Lasso) and L2 (Ridge) regularization 25 , allowing correlated predictors to be retained while shrinking predictors with limited contribution.
text.formatted: Elastic net combines L1 (Lasso) and L2 (Ridge) regularization <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25</ref> , allowing correlated predictors to be retained while shrinking predictors with limited contribution.

text.text: This property is advantageous for proteomic data, in which correlated biomarkers may reflect overlapping biological pathways.
Analyses were performed in Python 3.11 using ElasticNet from scikit-learn 1.7.
The outcome was twoyear change in the global cognitive composite score.
As Elastic Net penalization is scale-dependent, all predictors were standardized (z-scored) using the mean and SD estimated from the training fold.
Model robustness was assessed using nested cross-validation, with an outer 4-fold loop for performance evaluation and an inner 3-fold loop for hyperparameter tuning.
A 4-fold outer split was chosen to preserve adequate per-fold sample size given the limited size of the study cohort, particularly for the control-only and intervention-only analyses.

11 For each outer training fold, hyperparameters were optimized with a randomized search, by minimizing mean squared error (MSE) on the inner validation folds: the regularization strength (alpha) was searched on a logarithmic scale from 10 to 10², and the L1/L2 mixing ratio (l1_ratio) was searched uniformly between 0.1 and 1.0.

Candidate hyperparameter combinations yielding fewer than five non-zero coefficients were excluded from consideration, to avoid overly sparse, unstable models and balance predictive performance against biological interpretability.
For each outer fold, one final elastic net model was fit on the full outer training set using the selected hyperparameters, yielding four models per cohort.
Predictive performance was evaluated on each corresponding outer test fold using MSE, reported as mean ± SD across the four outer folds.

Predictor robustness was evaluated using two complementary perspectives, computed across the four fold-specific final models: (i) coefficient magnitude, reflecting each biomarker's direct contribution to predicted cognitive change within a given fold's model; (ii) shrinkage resistance, defined as the regularization strength (alpha) at which each biomarker's coefficient first reached zero along the Elastic net regularization path, with higher thresholds indicating greater robustness to penalization and lower likelihood of representing noise.

Attention was paid to biomarkers nominally significant in mixed-effects models, repeatedly selected across Elastic Net folds with large coefficient magnitudes and persistent under strong regularization.

The future of dementia prevention will likely require approaches that can be tailored to individuals' biological profiles and possibly integrated with disease-modifying therapies.

FINGER, the first large multidomain lifestyle trial to demonstrate cognitive benefits in older adults at increased risk of dementia, provides a unique opportunity to investigate the molecular correlates of intervention response.

Through longitudinal profiling of a panel of exploratory blood proteins quantified before and after the two-year intervention period, we identified changes in proteins involved in inflammation, synaptic integrity, pathological protein aggregation, vascular-and metabolic-processes with greatest effects on CRH, IL7 and MME.
Several baseline proteins modified the cognitive response to the FINGER intervention, suggesting biological determinants of intervention responsiveness.
Additional proteins exhibited APOE ε4-or sex-dependent effect modification, revealing heterogeneity in the biological mechanisms associated with cognitive response.

Several proteins associated with intervention-related outcomes showed significant correlations with established ADRDs, although these associations were generally modest, suggesting that the biological pathways they reflect may partly overlap with, but are not fully captured by traditional ADRD biomarkers.
Supporting these findings, machine learning analyses integrating multiple biomarkers and participant characteristics identified multivariable signatures predictive of intervention benefit.

Finally, comparison of baseline biomarker profiles between intervention-adherent responders and non-responders provided further biological insight into pathways that may contribute to favorable cognitive outcomes following multidomain lifestyle intervention.

Given the limited availability of accessible biomarkers for predicting cognitive decline in older adults without dementia, we first examined associations between baseline plasma proteins and longitudinal cognition in the total FINGER cohort, adjusting for randomization group.
We found that a set of proteins predicted less favorable longitudinal cognitive outcomes independent of intervention assignment.
These markers are related to immune-and inflammatory processes 26 , neurodegeneration pathways, synaptic integrity 27, 28 , and metabolic regulation 29 .

text.formatted: Levels of MME in the periphery, however, are generally elevated in association with poor metabolic health <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35</ref> consistent with its role in the regulation of multiple metabolic and vascular proteins including incretins (e.g. glucagon-like peptide-1, GLP-1 <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">36</ref> ).

text.text: Thus, the intervention-related reduction in circulating MME may reflect favorable changes in peripheral metabolic regulation rather than diminished cerebral Aβ clearance.
CRH was found to be increased by the FINGER intervention.
CRH is produced in the hypothalamus where it induces release of corticosteroids 37, 38 .
text.formatted: CRH is produced in the hypothalamus where it induces release of corticosteroids <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">37,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">38</ref> .

text.text: This stress related hormone has previously been shown to be decreased in plasma across several age-related neurodegenerative disorders 39, 40 and in postmortem brain material from AD patients 41, 42 , plausibly resulting from a general endocrine insufficiency and/or a negative feedback loop from cortisol over-activation.

text.text: Furthermore, CRH is increased with physical exercise and with stress 43 , and is also linked with inflammation, energy homeostasis and metabolism 44 .
text.formatted: Furthermore, CRH is increased with physical exercise and with stress <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">43</ref> , and is also linked with inflammation, energy homeostasis and metabolism <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">44</ref> .

text.text: The observed increase in circulating CRH may therefore reflect an adaptation in the participants' general metabolic and immune health, in alignment with the FINGER model.
However, increased activation of stress-response pathways remains an alternative explanation, and further investigation is needed to establish the physiological significance of these protein changes.

Thus, these results suggest that the early biological effects of multidomain lifestyle intervention may involve neuroendocrine, immune and metabolic processes not adequately captured by conventional markers of amyloid and tau pathology, at least over a two-year period in older adults at increased dementia risk.

Several baseline proteins modified the association between the intervention and subsequent cognitive trajectories, suggesting that the cognitive response to multidomain intervention may differ according to the underlying biological profile.

Kinase insert domain receptor (KDR/VEGFR2), a key receptor involved in angiogenesis and vascular function 45 , was the strongest effect modifier among the proteins analysed, with higher baseline levels predicting more cognitive improvement under intervention.

text.text: Interestingly, KDR peripheral levels were previously found lower in individuals with dementia compared to healthy controls, and decreased mRNA levels were observed in the brain of AD mouse models 46 .
text.formatted: Interestingly, KDR peripheral levels were previously found lower in individuals with dementia compared to healthy controls, and decreased mRNA levels were observed in the brain of AD mouse models <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">46</ref> .

text.text: This may suggest that differences in vascular and angiogenic signalling are relevant to the capacity to respond to lifestyle modification.

Several other identified effect modifying proteins were related to synaptic function and neurotrophic signalling (PTN, NPTX1, BDNF, GDNF and SNAP25) [47] [48] [49] or immune and inflammatory processes (CCL2, TREM2 and IL7) 50 .

text.text: Importantly, the direction of these associations differed across proteins, suggesting that both baseline vulnerability and resilience may shape the potential for intervention benefit.

Some protein profiles may reflect biological vulnerability that remains modifiable through lifestyle intervention, whereas others may indicate more established processes with less potential for modification, or conversely a more resilient state with less room for additional benefit.

This was apparent among neurotrophic proteins: the unfavourable association of higher BDNF with cognitive trajectories in controls was attenuated under intervention, whereas GDNF showed a more favourable association in controls but a less favourable pattern in intervention participants.
In contrast, higher baseline TREM2 was associated with poorer cognitive trajectories in both groups, with a more pronounced negative association under intervention.

Given the role of TREM2 in microglial responses and AD-related neurodegeneration 51 , higher circulating levels may identify a state of greater underlying disease or immune-related vulnerability that is less amenable to modification through lifestyle intervention.
CRH also emerged as an effect modifier, with higher baseline levels associated with a more favourable cognitive trajectory under intervention.

Whereas our previous FINGER analysis found no significant effect modification by established plasma ADRD biomarkers 17 , the present study highlights candidate synaptic, vascular, immune and neuroendocrine pathways that may contribute to heterogeneity in cognitive responses to multidomain lifestyle intervention.

text.text: The heterogeneous associations observed across these proteins suggest that intervention responsiveness may depend on multiple interacting biological processes rather than individual biomarkers in isolation.

To explore this possibility, we complemented the mixed-effects analyses with machine-learning approaches integrating the broader proteomic panel, established ADRD biomarkers and participant characteristics.
P-tau217 was one of the most consistently selected predictors of cognitive change, supporting its established prognostic relevance 52 .
text.formatted: P-tau217 was one of the most consistently selected predictors of cognitive change, supporting its established prognostic relevance <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">52</ref> .

text.text: In contrast, CRH, CCL2 and PTN showed more intervention-dependent patterns, contributing prominently to predictions in the intervention group but less consistently in controls.
Their interaction terms were also repeatedly retained in full-cohort models, providing complementary support for the effect modification observed in the mixed-effects analyses.

Together, these findings suggest that CRH, CCL2 and PTN warrant further investigation as candidate biomarkers of differential intervention responsiveness, whereas p-tau217 may primarily capture broader cognitive vulnerability.
Non-modifiable individual characteristics may influence the associations between biomarkers and responsiveness to lifestyle interventions.
We therefore, investigated whether baseline plasma proteins modified the FINGER intervention on cognitive trajectories according to APOE ε4 carrier status and sex.
These analyses identified additional effect modifiers particularly in APOE ε4 carriers.

Higher baseline levels of proteins related to proteinopathies (HTT, TARDBP and SNCA) were associated with less favorable cognitive change in the control group, an effect that was neutralized by the intervention.
These biomarkers were highly inter-correlated which could potentially be due to an overlapping biology.

The APOE ε4 variant has been recognized as a mediator of "systemic biological vulnerability" across neurodegenerative disorders by altering inflammatory profiles 53 and impairing neuronal protein degradation systems 54, 55 .
text.formatted: The APOE ε4 variant has been recognized as a mediator of "systemic biological vulnerability" across neurodegenerative disorders by altering inflammatory profiles <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">53</ref> and impairing neuronal protein degradation systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">54,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">55</ref> .

text.text: In this context, our findings indicate that multidomain intervention may partly counteract cognitive vulnerability associated with these processes in APOE ε4 carriers, offering insights for future tailoring of interventions according to genetic risk.

A recent meta-analysis has also shown that APOE ε4 carriers benefit more from lifestyle-based dementia risk reduction strategies 56 which may at least partially be due to the herein identified effects.
text.formatted: A recent meta-analysis has also shown that APOE ε4 carriers benefit more from lifestyle-based dementia risk reduction strategies <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">56</ref> which may at least partially be due to the herein identified effects.

text.text: Given their higher risk of dementia and potential side effects from anti-amyloid treatment, APOE ε4 carriers represent a prioritized group which could be particularly relevant for future precision prevention strategies.
The impact of sex on effect modification revealed four biomarkers with differential associations with cognitive response between men and women.
In women, the intervention attenuated a negative association of PARK7 (DJ-1) and a positive association of CSF2 with cognitive change.
In men, CXCL8 was associated with poorer cognitive trajectories in the control group, whereas IL6R was positively associated with cognitive change.

Three out of four proteins were inflammatory; however no sex differences were observed for the many other inflammatory proteins assessed, suggesting that there is not a general sex-dependent inflammatory-related effect modification.
In future analyses, a broader range of biomarkers may provide additional insight into potential sex-dependent differences.

To further characterize the biological profiles associated with favourable cognitive outcomes, we compared baseline plasma proteins between cognitive responders and non-responders among highly adherent FINGER intervention participants.

Higher baseline levels of KDR, BDNF and PTN were associated with greater odds of cognitive improvement, potentially implicating vascular and neurotrophic pathways in cognitive outcomes following multidomain lifestyle intervention.
Immune-related proteins showed contrasting associations, with higher TREM2 and IL12p70 associated with lower odds of improvement, whereas CCL2, CXCL1 and IL17A showed positive associations.
This suggests that distinct immune pathways, rather than a uniform inflammatory profile, may be relevant to cognitive response.
Higher baseline REST was also associated with lower odds of improvement.
REST has been implicated in neuronal stress resistance and neuroprotection 57 and shown to be increased following mindfulness-based stress reduction 58 .
text.formatted: REST has been implicated in neuronal stress resistance and neuroprotection <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">57</ref> and shown to be increased following mindfulness-based stress reduction <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">58</ref> .

text.text: In our cohort, however, higher REST correlated with older age and several established ADRD biomarkers, despite showing no significant associations with cognitive trajectories.
These findings raise the possibility that circulating REST reflects age-related biological vulnerability or compensatory stress responses, although its physiological significance remains uncertain.
This study has several strengths.
It represents a unique investigation of circulating proteomic markers within a randomized controlled multidomain lifestyle intervention.

The relatively large and deeply phenotyped FINGER cohort, together with longitudinal cognitive assessments, allowed us to examine both changes in biomarkers following the intervention and their associations with cognitive trajectories.

The use of highly sensitive NULISA technology enabled the measurement of a broad range of proteins, including low-abundance circulating proteins that may not be captured by conventional proteomic approaches.

Finally, the combination of mixed-effects models and Elastic Net provided two complementary approaches to identify intervention-related biomarker signals, while nested crossvalidation was used to improve the robustness of the machine-learning analyses.
Some limitations should also be considered.

First, although the FINGER trial included a relatively large cohort, statistical power to detect protein-intervention interactions was limited, particularly for the more complex four-way interactions involving APOE ε4 status or sex.

These exploratory analyses were not based on prespecified protein-specific hypotheses, and their interpretation is challenging given the number of comparisons and potential instability of higher-order interaction estimates.

Several of the findings, particularly from the intervention and interaction analyses, did not survive correction for multiple testing and should therefore be considered exploratory and require replication.

Although Elastic Net provided a complementary way to assess the consistency of the biomarker signals identified in the mixed-effects analyses, evidence of overfitting and the absence of an external validation cohort, limit the generalizability of the findings.

Second, the FINGER eligibility criteria selected older adults at increased dementia risk with cognitive performance within a relatively restricted range, potentially limiting the generalizability of the findings and influencing cross-sectional associations between proteins and cognition.
Furthermore, the responder analyses were restricted to highly adherent intervention participants.
As adherence may be associated with participant characteristics influencing cognitive outcomes, these results should be interpreted cautiously.
Finally, the relatively homogeneous Finnish study population may limit generalizability to more ethnically and socioeconomically diverse populations.
Future studies should prioritize adequately powered, hypothesis-driven analyses and independent validation of candidate biomarkers and predictive models across diverse populations.

The Finnish Geriatric Intervention Study to Prevent Cognitive Impairment and Disability (FINGER) randomized 1,260 older adults at increased risk of dementia to a 2-year multidomain lifestyle intervention (n = 631) or a control group receiving regular health advice (n = 629).
The intervention comprised nutritional guidance, physical activity, cognitive training, social interaction and vascular risk management.

Plasma samples collected at baseline and the 2-year follow-up were analyzed using the NULISA CNS 120 multiplex proteomic assay, covering proteins involved in neurodegeneration, synaptic function, vascular biology, amyloid and tau pathology, inflammation and metabolism.

Statistical modeling and machine-learning approaches were used to investigate intervention-related changes in circulating proteins, associations with cognitive outcomes and baseline protein predictors of cognitive response to the intervention, with the aim of informing personalized dementia prevention strategies.
